opus-5.5.text:
I think the basic idea is sensible, and it's broadly in the direction a lot of us have been thinking. At DeepMind we've worked on what we call a Frontier Safety Framework. You define certain capability thresholds, things like significant uplift in cyber offense, or a system that can meaningfully help someone build a biological weapon, or a system with strong autonomous capabilities. Before you deploy, or even keep scaling past a point, you need appropriate mitigations in place. If you can't get them in place, you shouldn't proceed in that way.

The hard part is in the details. First, measurement. Our evaluations are still fairly immature. It's hard to know whether you've actually elicited a model's full capabilities, or whether some clever prompting or fine-tuning would reveal it can do much more than your tests showed. So there's a real risk of false confidence. A lot of work has to go into making these evaluations rigorous and trustworthy.

Second, defining what "safe enough" means at each level. Saying you'll pause if safety benchmarks aren't met is easy. Specifying those benchmarks so they're meaningful, not just box-ticking, is much harder, especially for things like deceptive alignment, where the failure mode is precisely that the system looks fine on your tests.

Third, coordination. If one lab pauses and others don't, you haven't necessarily made the world safer. You may just have shifted where the frontier is. So frameworks like this become much more powerful when they're shared across the industry and eventually backed by governments in some form, so everyone is held to comparable standards.

So overall I'm supportive. I think it's one of the more practical tools we have right now. But I'd frame it as a starting point. It needs to mature quickly, because capabilities are moving fast, and we want these mechanisms working well before we reach the really dangerous levels, not scrambling to build them when we're already there.

r001.rationale: The response says that defining what “safe enough” means at each capability level is difficult, and that benchmarks must be meaningful rather than box-ticking.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the general shape of that is quite reasonable, and honestly it's roughly the direction we've been moving in at DeepMind and across the industry with things like the Frontier Safety Framework. The core idea is that you shouldn't be reasoning about risk in the abstract. You should be saying: here are specific capabilities that, if a system had them, would be concerning — things like meaningful uplift on biological or chemical weapons, serious cyber-offensive capability, the ability to autonomously replicate and acquire resources, or deceptive behaviour that's robust to our oversight. And then you tie your evaluations to those thresholds and you commit, in advance, to what you're going to do if a model crosses them.

Where I'd push a little is on the word "benchmark." A benchmark sounds like a fixed test with a number you pass or fail, and the problem is that capability evaluations are genuinely hard. Models can sandbag, evals can saturate or get contaminated, and the thing you're measuring might not be the thing that actually matters. So I'd want these to be more like a set of evaluations plus a process — red-teaming, external review, some humility about what the numbers mean — rather than a single score that lets you tick a box and move on. If you make it too mechanical, you get people optimising to clear the hurdle rather than actually understanding the system.

The pause-or-slow-down part I think is right in principle. If you hit a critical capability and you don't have the mitigations in place — the security, the deployment controls, the alignment work — then you shouldn't deploy it, and arguably you should be cautious about continuing to scale it. The practical difficulty is that a unilateral pause by one lab doesn't really solve the problem if others carry on. That's why I think this ultimately needs some coordination, whether that's through governments, international bodies, or at least shared industry standards, so that the response is roughly consistent regardless of who hits the threshold first.

The other thing I'd say is that we're at a point where the capabilities are advancing quickly enough that these frameworks need to exist before we need them. You don't want to be designing the fire exits while the building is on fire. So I'm quite supportive of putting concrete, if imperfect, thresholds in place now and then iterating on them as our understanding improves. The alternative — waiting until we've got perfect measures — basically means waiting until it's too late.

r001.rationale: The response explains why concrete safety requirements are difficult to specify: capability evaluations can be hard to design and interpret, models may sandbag, evaluations may saturate or be contaminated, and a measured score may miss the relevant risk.

astra-6.text:
I think that’s broadly a sensible approach. As these systems become more capable, the evidence we require that they’re safe should become stronger. And if you reach a level of capability where you can’t provide that evidence, there needs to be a meaningful consequence—including slowing down or pausing further development.

The difficult part is specifying the benchmarks. We don’t have a complete science of evaluating these systems, and passing a particular set of tests doesn’t establish that a system is safe. So I’d want a framework that can evolve as we learn, with independent scrutiny of whether the tests are actually measuring the risks we care about.

You also want to agree on those conditions in advance. If you wait until you have a very powerful system and there’s enormous commercial pressure to deploy it, that’s a much harder moment to decide where the boundary should be.

r001.rationale: The response explicitly says “the difficult part is specifying the benchmarks” for a framework that requires stronger safety evidence at greater capability levels and may slow or pause development if that evidence is lacking.

sol-6.1.text:
I think that’s a sensible general approach. As systems become more capable, the evidence we require that they’re safe should become stronger. And if we can’t produce that evidence, we should be prepared to slow down or pause further development.

The difficult part is making the benchmarks meaningful. You don’t want a situation where a system passes a collection of tests and everybody concludes that it must therefore be safe. You need to understand what those tests establish, what they miss, and whether they’re still adequate for the next level of capability.

So I’d support a framework like that, provided it can evolve as we learn more. The thresholds need to be concrete enough to constrain decisions, but we shouldn’t pretend that we already know how to measure every important risk.

r001.rationale: The response says the difficult part is making benchmarks meaningful, explaining that tests have limits and must remain adequate as capability rises. It also notes that thresholds should be concrete enough to constrain decisions.
